sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

content.text:
Create an animated, non-interactive surfing pelican using html/3js

Build this as an interactive web page in the current directory.
- The entry point is index.html. Put your code in JavaScript ES modules loaded from it
  (`<script type="module" src="main.js">`), and add a short README.md.
- You may use npm packages: `npm install <package>` here, then import them by name
  (`import * as THREE from "three"`). No CDN URLs and no import maps.
- Afterwards the page is packaged into one self-contained index.html with esbuild: every script and
  stylesheet index.html references is bundled with everything it imports. Load assets the page needs
  with `import` (they become data URLs) or generate them in code, never by URL string.
- The packaged page runs offline in a sandboxed iframe: no network requests, and no localStorage,
  cookies or other storage (they throw there).
- Check that it packages: `esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null` must succeed.
  Don't build or package the page yourself; that happens afterwards.
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory.
- Finish with a short summary of what you built.

# Surfing Pelican 🌊🦩

An animated, non-interactive 3D scene built with [Three.js](https://threejs.org/).

A pelican in sunglasses rides a wave on a surfboard while the camera slowly
orbits the scene. Everything is generated procedurally in code — no external
assets.

## What's in the scene

- **Procedural ocean** — a displaced plane whose vertices follow an analytic
  sum-of-sines wave field, with flat shading for a stylized look.
- **Surfing pelican** — built entirely from primitives (spheres, cones,
  tubes). It bobs with the swell, carves the board left and right, flaps its
  wings in bursts, and occasionally squawks (the throat pouch stretches).
- **Board physics-lite** — the surfboard samples the same wave function and
  pitches/rolls to match the wave slope.
- **Splash particles** — spawned at the board's tail as it cuts through water.
- **Environment** — gradient sky dome, sun disc, drifting cloud billboards,
  warm directional light with soft shadows, and distance fog.
- **Camera** — a slow cinematic orbit that follows the pelican with a subtle
  hand-held sway.

## Running

Open `index.html` with any static server (the page uses ES modules):

```sh
npx serve .
# or
python3 -m http.server
```

The scene is non-interactive by design: just watch the pelican surf.

## Files

- `index.html` — entry point, loads the module script
- `main.js` — the whole scene: lighting, ocean, pelican, particles, animation

content.text:
All checks pass. Here's what I built:

## Summary

**Surfing Pelican** — an animated, non-interactive 3D scene in Three.js:

**Files**
- `index.html` — entry point loading `main.js` as an ES module
- `main.js` — the entire scene (~380 lines, `three` imported by name from npm)
- `README.md` — short overview and run instructions

**Scene highlights**
- **Procedural ocean**: a 240×240 plane whose vertices are displaced by an analytic sum-of-sines wave field (flat-shaded Phong for a stylized look), with the same function sampled for the rider
- **Surfing pelican** built entirely from primitives: egg body, curved tube neck, long orange bill with a stretchable throat pouch, flapping wings on shoulder pivots, tail feathers, webbed feet — plus sunglasses
- **Riding motion**: the board carves a smooth loop across the ocean, pitching and rolling to match the local wave slope via finite differences; the pelican bobs, leans, flaps in periodic bursts, and occasionally squawks (pouch stretches wide)
- **Splash particles**: 60 recycled droplets spawned at the board's tail with gravity and fade-out
- **Environment**: code-generated gradient sky dome, sun disc, drifting cloud billboards, warm shadow-casting directional light + hemisphere fill, distance fog
- **Camera**: slow cinematic orbit that tracks the board with a subtle hand-held sway

No network requests, no storage use, and all textures (sky gradient, clouds) are generated in code via canvas — so it packages cleanly with esbuild (verified: `esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm` succeeds).
